summary: Jesus compares the kingdom to hidden treasure, a priceless pearl and a dragnet, then likens His instructed disciples to a householder bringing out treasures new and old.
key_insight: One man stumbles on the treasure; the other searches until he finds the pearl. They come to the kingdom by different roads, but both sell everything to have it, and the first does it “for joy.”
story: In the house, Jesus went on teaching His disciples. “The kingdom of heaven is like treasure hidden in a field, which a man found and hid; and for joy over it he goes and sells all that he has and buys that field.”
Again, the kingdom is like a merchant seeking beautiful pearls. When he found one pearl of great price, he went and sold all that he had and bought it.

Again, it is like a dragnet cast into the sea that gathered fish of every kind. When it was full, the fishermen drew it to shore, sat down, gathered the good into vessels and threw the bad away. “So it will be at the end of the age. The angels will come forth, separate the wicked from among the just, and cast them into the furnace of fire.”

Jesus asked them, “Have you understood all these things?” They said, “Yes, Lord.” Then He said, “Therefore every scribe instructed concerning the kingdom of heaven is like a householder who brings out of his treasure things new and old.”
When Jesus had finished these parables, He left that place.

scene.label: Where?
scene.text: Matthew last placed Jesus in the house with His disciples, away from the crowds by the sea (13:36), and only after these parables does He depart from there (13:53). So these parables, and the question “Have you understood all these things?”, were most likely spoken in the house in Capernaum, to the disciples alone.

scene.label: Buried treasure
scene.text: With no banks and frequent wars, people hid valuables in the ground (compare Matthew 25:25). If the owner died or fled, a hoard could lie forgotten for generations until a plow struck it.

scene.label: Pearls
scene.text: Pearls came from the Persian Gulf, the Red Sea and the Indian Ocean, and in the Roman world they were among the costliest of all luxuries. A merchant who dealt in them knew a rare one when he saw it.

scene.label: The dragnet
scene.text: A dragnet was a long net with floats along the top and weights along the bottom. Fishermen drew it through the water and hauled it onto the beach, catching everything in its path.

scene.label: Good and bad fish
scene.text: The Law allowed Israel to eat only water creatures with fins and scales (Leviticus 11:9–12). On the shore, fishermen sorted out the unclean and worthless catch and threw it away.

witnesses.matthew: Only Matthew records these parables. They close his chapter of seven parables, pairing the joy of finding the kingdom with the certainty of final judgment. The saying about the scribe who brings out “things new and old” may describe Matthew’s own work, for he constantly shows the old Scriptures fulfilled in Jesus.

seeing.reveals: Jesus presents the kingdom, and so Himself as its King, as worth more than everything a person owns. He also speaks plainly of a final sorting that His angels will carry out.
seeing.living: Following Jesus costs everything, but the man in the field does not sell in grief; he sells “for joy.” Whatever you let go to have Christ is a trade, not a loss. And because the net will be sorted, the time to come to Him is now.
seeing.ponder: What are you still holding that you would gladly let go if you saw the kingdom as the treasure Jesus says it is?

preaching.big_idea: The kingdom is worth everything, and those who truly find it give everything gladly.
outline: Sorted at the end: the net (47–50)
preaching.watch_for: The treasure and the pearl are a matched pair, each ending with a man who sells all that he has. The net then repeats the close of the tares explanation almost word for word (13:42, 50). The kingdom is worth everything now because a final sorting is coming.

title: The Treasure, the Pearl and the Net
